title: Heterogeneity and predictors of the effects of AI assistance on radiologists
author: Feiyang Yu · Alex Moehring · Oishi Banerjee · Tobias Salz · Nikhil Agarwal · Pranav Rajpurkar

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Clinical teaming: AI accuracy may worsen joint decisions
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core caution against assuming human involvement or seniority ensures benefit and materially develops it with individual-level evidence: assistance effects vary substantially, experience-based characteristics are unreliable predictors, inaccurate AI can worsen performance, and deployment should test each radiologist under realistic, locally representative conditions.
qs: We found that experience-based radiologist characteristics, including years of experience, subspecialty in thoracic radiology and experience with AI tools, did not serve as reliable predictors of treatment effect, in terms of both calibration performance and discrimination performance.

Without reliable predictors, it is necessary to measure radiologists’ response to AI assistance under realistic simulations of deployment settings before deciding whether to provide AI assistance to different radiologists.

st.t: Radiology assistance: Accuracy, teamwork and replacement diverge
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s distinction between AI capability and effective human assistance, and materially develops it with evidence that assistance effects vary across radiologists, conventional experience measures do not reliably predict benefit, and inaccurate AI advice can reduce performance. It further proposes personalized collaboration and improved model accuracy as conditional deployment priorities, without claiming demonstrated workforce replacement or successful clinical deployment.
qs: Surprisingly, conventional experience-based factors, such as years of experience, subspecialty and familiarity with AI tools, fail to reliably predict the impact of AI assistance.

Instead, we found that the occurrence of AI errors strongly influences treatment outcomes, with inaccurate AI predictions adversely affecting radiologist performance on the aggregate of all pathologies and on half of the individual pathologies investigated.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The study accepts and materially strengthens the cluster’s central claim that AI assistance is heterogeneous and must be deployed selectively. Large-scale radiology evidence shows that effects vary across users and tasks, conventional experience or baseline skill poorly predicts benefit, and realistic, deployment-specific testing is preferable to uniform allocation. Although outside legal practice, it provides concrete cross-domain evidence for task- and user-specific evaluation and calibrated human oversight.
qs: Our findings, based on a large-scale sample of 140 radiologists, highlight the existence of radiologist heterogeneity in treatment effects, which has substantial implications for both absolute and relative performance.

Without reliable predictors, it is necessary to measure radiologists’ response to AI assistance under realistic simulations of deployment settings before deciding whether to provide AI assistance to different radiologists.

st.t: Human-AI decisions: Self-knowledge conditions unrealized gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal claim that AI assistance is not uniformly beneficial: effects vary across radiologists, large model errors can produce substantial harm, and standard traits such as experience or baseline skill do not reliably predict benefit. It therefore endorses realistic, individualized workflow testing before deployment, while not itself establishing self-knowledge or self-calibration as the mechanism.
qs: More accurate AI predictions led to higher treatment effects: AI assistance with absolute error under 20 resulted in a treatment effect of 0.679 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.492 to 0.865, n  = 176,130; Supplementary Table 11 ), whereas AI assistance with absolute error above 80 resulted in a treatment effect of −16.845 (95% CI: −24.288 to −9.403, n  = 371).

Without reliable predictors, it is necessary to measure radiologists’ response to AI assistance under realistic simulations of deployment settings before deciding whether to provide AI assistance to different radiologists.

kp.k: Study examines heterogeneous assistance effects across 140 radiologists
kp.d: This medical-domain study analyzed 140 radiologists interpreting 324 retrospective Stanford patient cases across 15 chest X-ray diagnostic tasks. The non-repeated-measure design included 107 radiologists, each reading 30 cases unassisted and 30 assisted; 33 radiologists in the repeated-measure design read 60 cases under each of four AI/clinical-history conditions, producing 240 diagnoses each. Conditions were randomized, with a 2-week washout between repeated-measure sessions. The analysis combined clinical-history conditions and studied diagnostic performance, not legal work.
qs: We analyzed data collected using a diagnostic study involving 140 radiologists, 324 patient cases and 15 pathologies with corresponding AI predictions from two study designs: one with repeated measurements on the same case and one without
Each radiologist read a total of 60 patient cases, each under each of the four treatment conditions and producing a total of 240 diagnoses.

kp.k: Assistance provided probabilities rather than explanations or autonomous decisions
kp.d: Radiologists received CheXpert predictions for all 15 pathologies simultaneously, alongside chest X-rays and, where applicable, clinical histories. Predictions were probabilities on a 0–100 scale, without explanations or pathology localization. Before participation, radiologists received model information, interface training, comprehension checks and practice cases containing predictions from the experimental model.
qs: The AI predictions were presented in the form of prediction probabilities on a 0–100 scale.
Participating radiologists received onboarding training on the assistive AI system before starting the experiment and were shown example AI predictions from the same AI model used in the experiment
the AI assistance available to radiologists contained only predicted probabilities and did not include additional explanations, such as localization of pathologies

kp.k: Performance measures distinguish probability error from discrimination
kp.d: The primary outcome was improvement in absolute error: unassisted error minus assisted error, using the absolute difference between predicted and reference probabilities on a 0–100 scale. Reference probabilities averaged assessments by five board-certified Mount Sinai chest radiologists with at least 10 years of experience. Discrimination was assessed separately using AUROC, with reference probabilities thresholded at 50; AUROC treatment effects were assisted minus unassisted AUROC.
qs: Absolute error was defined as the absolute difference between the radiologist-predicted probability and the ground truth probability on a 0–100 scale.

The ground truth probabilities for a patient case were determined by averaging the continuous predicted probabilities of five board-certified radiologists from Mount Sinai Hospital with at least 10 years of experience and chest radiology as a subspecialty on a 0–100 scale.

kp.k: AI assistance helps some radiologists and harms others
kp.d: Individual treatment effects across all pathologies ranged from −1.295 to 1.440 absolute-error points (IQR, 0.797). For detecting abnormal chest X-rays, the range was −8.914 to 5.563 (IQR, 3.245). The authors interpret this variation as consequential for absolute performance and relative standing. They used empirical Bayes shrinkage to reduce overestimation of heterogeneity caused by sampling error.
qs: Our findings revealed substantial heterogeneity in the treatment effects of AI assistance among different radiologists
the largest range of treatment effects extended from −8.914 to 5.563 (IQR, 3.245) for detecting whether chest X-rays are abnormal.
We used the empirical Bayes method

kp.k: Experience and specialization do not reliably predict assistance benefits
kp.d: Among 136 survey respondents, years of experience, thoracic subspecialization and prior AI-tool experience failed to reliably predict treatment effects, individually or in a combined model. Experience was divided at the median of 6 years. Aggregate subgroup differences were not statistically significant for either absolute error or AUROC; individual-pathology differences did not survive Benjamini–Hochberg correction. These findings challenge reported experience-based associations without establishing that experience can never matter in other settings.
qs: We found that experience-based radiologist characteristics, including years of experience, subspecialty in thoracic radiology and experience with AI tools, did not serve as reliable predictors of treatment effect, in terms of both calibration performance and discrimination performance.
These characteristics were collected through a post-experiment survey completed by 136 radiologists.

kp.k: Lower baseline performers do not consistently benefit more
kp.d: Using separate case samples and adjustment for attenuation bias, unassisted absolute error had a positive but statistically insignificant association with assistance gains across all pathologies. Individual-pathology associations were not significant after multiple-testing correction. Unassisted AUROC likewise did not significantly predict AUROC gains in aggregate. Thus, measured baseline diagnostic skill did not reliably identify who would benefit most.
qs: Surprisingly, radiologists who initially performed poorly without AI assistance did not necessarily benefit more or experience more harm from AI assistance compared to higher-performing counterparts.
We employed a split sampling approach, using distinct sets of patient cases to calculate the unassisted error and treatment effect.

kp.k: Shared measurement noise creates spurious equalization findings
kp.d: The authors demonstrate that calculating baseline error and improvement from overlapping cases creates a spurious relationship through reversion to the mean. Their naive aggregate model produced statistically significant coefficients of 0.357 after attenuation adjustment and 0.309 without adjustment (both P < 0.001), unlike the split-sample analysis. Analogous spurious negative associations appeared for baseline AUROC and AUROC gains. This is a statistical measurement issue, not fabricated generative-model output.
qs: This phenomenon, therefore, falsely creates a positive correlation between unassisted error and treatment effect (unassisted error minus assisted error).
Split sampling prevents reversion to the mean by using disjoint patient cases to compute unassisted error and treatment effect for each data point in the linear regression model.

kp.k: Stronger baseline performance generally persists with AI assistance
kp.d: Although baseline performance poorly predicted improvement, it predicted assisted performance. Split-sample regressions adjusted for attenuation bias showed significant aggregate associations for absolute error and AUROC (P < 0.001). Absolute-error associations remained significant for most individual pathologies, except atelectasis, pneumothorax and shoulder fracture after correction. The findings support persistence of relative diagnostic performance rather than consistent equalization.
qs: Together, these findings indicate that unassisted error serves as a strong predictor of assisted error in most cases.
To again avoid reversion to the mean, we adopted a split sampling approach in which we used separate sets of patient cases to compute unassisted error and assisted error for each radiologist.

kp.k: Large AI errors can substantially worsen clinician performance
kp.d: Across pathologies, AI predictions with absolute error under 20 were associated with an improvement of 0.679 (95% CI: 0.492 to 0.865; n = 176,130), whereas error above 80 was associated with deterioration of −16.845 (95% CI: −24.288 to −9.403; n = 371). Differences across error bins were significant (P < 0.001). The authors interpret these results as suggesting that radiologists cannot consistently distinguish accurate from inaccurate predictions and may be misled.
qs: Conversely, AI predictions with large errors tend to lead to negative treatment effects, suggesting that radiologists struggle to consistently distinguish between accurate and inaccurate AI predictions and can be misled by inaccurate AI predictions.
More accurate AI predictions led to higher treatment effects

kp.k: Accuracy-benefit relationships vary across tasks and metrics
kp.d: More accurate AI predictions produced better absolute-error treatment effects for eight labels: abnormal, airspace opacity, cardiomediastinal abnormality, cardiomegaly, pleural effusion, pleural other, pneumothorax and support device hardware. Bacterial/lobar pneumonia and consolidation showed the reverse trend; remaining trends were unclear. AUROC effects varied significantly across aggregate AI-error bins, but the overall trend was unclear, and individual-pathology analysis was numerically feasible only for airspace opacity. Binary-reference analyses were broadly consistent, with specified exceptions.
qs: These findings suggest that AI error could be a predictor of treatment effect, but the statistical significance and direction of the relationship could differ across pathologies and metrics.
For individual pathologies, the AUROC analysis was numerically feasible only for airspace opacity, and the trend was unclear.

kp.k: Underestimation generally produces better effects than equivalent overestimation
kp.d: Across all pathologies, AI predictions understating reference probabilities produced better absolute-error treatment effects than equally large overstatements. Signed-error-bin differences were significant (P < 0.001). The underestimation advantage appeared for airspace opacity, atelectasis, cardiomegaly, consolidation and lesion, but no single pattern characterized all pathologies. AUROC analysis could not be repeated because most bins lacked both positive and negative cases.
qs: We observed that AI predictions with negative errors, indicating underestimation of probabilities by the AI, led to better treatment effects compared to predictions with the same magnitude of positive errors, indicating overestimation of probabilities by the AI
No singular trend was observed across individual pathologies.

kp.k: Deployment should test individual responses in representative settings
kp.d: The authors recommend individualized deployment rather than universal assistance or selection based solely on experience or baseline skill. Without reliable predictors, they propose measuring each radiologist’s response in realistic simulations using cases representative of the target population. Cognitive abilities, technological adaptability and decision-making processes are suggested for future predictor research, not demonstrated predictors in this study.
qs: Without reliable predictors, it is necessary to measure radiologists’ response to AI assistance under realistic simulations of deployment settings before deciding whether to provide AI assistance to different radiologists.
Future research should consider cognitive abilities, adaptability to new technologies and decision-making processes as potential predictors.

kp.k: Explanations and richer outputs remain untested improvement proposals
kp.d: Beyond increasing model accuracy, the authors suggest helping clinicians identify inaccurate predictions through explanations or nuanced radiology reports. These are proposed avenues rather than tested interventions. They recommend investigating explanation type and presentation while recognizing that additional information can increase cognitive burden.
qs: Apart from improving AI accuracy, it is valuable to help radiologists better identify inaccurate AI predictions.

Designers of AI systems should investigate the optimal types of explanations to present and the mode of presentation while staying cautious of the increased cognitive burden that this additional information can bring.

kp.k: Design limits causal mechanisms and learning-over-time conclusions
kp.d: The study could not assess whether clinicians improved at incorporating AI with experience over time. Simultaneous presentation of interrelated pathology predictions limited isolation of task-specific effects. Using actual predictions also left patient-case characteristics confounded with AI accuracy. The authors explicitly warn against treating accuracy-effect associations as explanations of the cognitive mechanism and call for controlled follow-up studies, potentially using artificially set predictions.
qs: We were unable to assess whether radiologists improved in incorporating AI predictions over time as they encountered more patient cases.
Therefore, these findings should not be extrapolated for defining the cognitive mechanism in which AI assistance helps or hurts radiologists.
Future work may control for the influence of the patient case by providing artificially set predictions to radiologists.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Yu and colleagues find heterogeneous effects of AI assistance on radiologists, rather than uniform improvement or consistent benefits for less-skilled practitioners.
pts.d: The authors report that AI assistance improved some radiologists' diagnostic performance and worsened others'. Across all pathologies, individual treatment effects on absolute error ranged from −1.295 to 1.440, with positive values indicating improvement. Years of experience, thoracic subspecialty and prior AI-tool experience did not reliably predict benefits, individually or in combination. Baseline diagnostic performance also poorly predicted the improvement from assistance after split sampling and multiple-testing correction. Nevertheless, stronger unassisted performers generally remained stronger assisted performers. These are findings about radiology assistance, not claims about legal services or replacement of professionals.

pts.k: The authors find that inaccurate AI predictions can worsen human performance, while the relationship between AI accuracy and benefit varies by pathology and performance metric.
pts.d: For aggregate absolute error, AI predictions with error under 20 produced an estimated improvement of 0.679 (95% CI 0.492 to 0.865), whereas predictions with error above 80 produced an estimated deterioration of −16.845 (95% CI −24.288 to −9.403). More accurate predictions yielded better treatment effects for roughly half the individual pathology labels, with reverse or unclear patterns for others. The aggregate AUROC relationship was not uniformly monotonic. At equal absolute error, underestimation of pathology probabilities generally produced better aggregate effects than overestimation. The authors interpret the negative effects of large AI errors as suggesting that radiologists can be misled, but explicitly decline to establish a cognitive mechanism from these associations.

pts.k: The authors recommend individualized deployment assessment and more accurate AI; explanations and richer reports are proposed possibilities rather than tested improvements.
pts.d: The authors argue that one-size-fits-all assistance is inadequate and recommend measuring individual clinicians' responses in realistic deployment simulations when reliable predictors are unavailable. They suggest that explanatory outputs or nuanced radiology reports might help clinicians extract value even from inaccurate predictions. That interface proposal was not tested in this experiment, which supplied probability predictions only; they also caution that additional information can increase cognitive burden.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on a diagnostic experiment involving 140 radiologists, 324 retrospective patient cases and 15 chest X-ray diagnostic tasks.
pts.d: Yu and colleagues analyze data from two randomized assistance designs: 107 radiologists each read 60 cases without repeating a case, and 33 each read 60 cases under four conditions, with two-week washouts between sessions. AI and clinical-history conditions were varied; the analysis pooled clinical-history conditions. CheXpert supplied probability predictions. Reference probabilities averaged judgments from five experienced board-certified thoracic radiologists. The primary outcome was improvement in absolute error on a 0–100 probability scale; AUROC assessed discrimination. Experience data came from 136 respondents. Empirical Bayes shrinkage addressed sampling-related overestimation of individual heterogeneity; split sampling addressed regression-to-the-mean artifacts; attenuation adjustments, clustered standard errors and multiple-testing corrections supported inference. The authors show that a naive analysis without split sampling produces spurious associations between baseline error and improvement. Their use of 'hallucinated correlation' describes a statistical artifact, not fabricated generative-AI content.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The March 2024 paper reports experimental findings, not a forecast with a deployment deadline or evidence of long-term adaptation.
pts.d: The findings concern radiologists using a specific chest X-ray prediction model after onboarding, with probabilities for all 15 labels presented simultaneously. They do not establish effects for other AI systems, explanatory interfaces, clinical tasks or patient populations. Randomized treatment ordering prevented analysis of learning over time. Interrelated pathology labels and simultaneous predictions limited isolation of individual-pathology effects. Actual model predictions also made it difficult to separate case characteristics from AI-error effects. The authors call for further controlled research and do not infer the cognitive mechanism by which assistance helps or harms. Prospective improvements from personalization, explanations and better models remain recommendations or possibilities without a specified timeframe.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected professionals are radiologists; the implementation implications concern healthcare organizations and AI developers, with patient benefits proposed rather than measured.
pts.d: The study addresses clinician augmentation: radiologists retain the diagnostic role while receiving AI probability predictions. Participants represented varied institutional settings, with recruitment through teleradiology companies and Vietnam's Vinmec health system. Individual clinicians may benefit or suffer reduced accuracy, and professional experience alone does not reliably identify which outcome to expect. Healthcare organizations are urged to assess individual responses, allocate training and assistance accordingly, and consider the target patient population. Developers are urged to improve model accuracy and investigate presentation formats. The study measures diagnostic performance rather than patient outcomes, employment displacement, costs or legal-market changes.
